title: Spartan
full_review:
A brutally efficient army commando becomes entangled in a deadly web of deception in the dense and dark thriller "Spartan" (Warner Bros.). Grafting his signature staccato dialogue onto a conventional search-and-rescue melodrama, writer-director David Mamet crafts an interesting, if not wholly satisfying, film -- part commercial pulp, part cerebral character study -- resulting in a highbrow action-adventure picture about duty and the dangers of blind obedience.

Val Kilmer stars as Robert Scott, a member of an elite special operations unit whose unquestioned commitment to his appointed missions has made him the government's go-to guy whenever they have a particularly dirty job. A career military man, Scott �put his conscience on ice� years ago, allowing him to employ unorthodox tactics in pursuing his goals -- like threatening to cut out a character's eye unless he divulges information.

Working with a highly secretive task force, jointly comprised of presidential advisers, FBI, CIA and Secret Service operatives, Scott is called in to rescue the president's daughter, Laura (Kristen Belle), after a botched security detail results in her being plucked from her Harvard dorm. Taken as a double feature with Mandy Moore's breezy teen comedy, "Chasing Liberty," it hasn't been a good year for first-daughter handlers.

Paired with Curtis (Derek Luke), a wet-behind-the-ears recruit, Scott is given the green light to go "off the meter" � use whatever means necessary � in hunting down Laura's kidnappers. He tracks them to a white slavery ring operating out of Dubai. But the straightforward story takes some twisting turns as their efforts become knotted by the murky machinations of shadowy impresarios, like Burch (Ed O'Neill) and Stoddard (an under-used William H. Macy), upper-echelon operatives who may know more than they are telling about the abduction.

Trading in his camouflage fatigues and night-vision goggles for some John Deere threads, Scott retires to his farm as he awaits his next assignment. Curtis, however, can't silence the inner voice that tells him Laura is still alive. He convinces Scott to resume the search, setting the two soldiers on a dangerous path and pulling them into a deadly vortex of conspiracy that reaches the highest corridors of power.

Not surprisingly, Mamet's stylized dialogue works against the film, giving what is essentially a noir actioner dressed up with some top-shelf tete-a-tete an overall feel of stilted theatricality and faux sophistication. It's as if Mamet wants to eat his popcorn and have it, too, to be both mainstream while maintaining his reputation as a serious "artist.�

Kilmer's contained performance effectively conveys Scott's steely implacability. Serving as the film's conscience, Luke imbues a palpable idealism.

Much of the potboiler's cabal-centered conceit echoes the conspiratorial canards and political paranoia of such films as "Three Days of the Condor" (1975), "The Parallax View" (1974) and "Enemy of the State" (1998). One of the main narrative threads of "Spartan" -- the media as a mechanism of manipulation and diversion -- is a darker variation of the theme explored in the black political comedy, "Wag the Dog" (1997), which Mamet also wrote.

The film also poses interesting questions. Scott is governed by an inflexible adherence to a warrior code that demands unflinching fealty to one's superiors. He considers neither the rightness nor wrongness of his actions; he simply follows orders. Early on he tells Curtis, "I ain't a thinker. I never wanted to be." For him, government sanction affirms the rectitude of his actions and justifies his unconventional -- at times savage -- ethics.

It is only after the search for the missing girl becomes a search for "the truth" that he begins to question the moral myopia that had made him so effective in his lethal line of work. And while the film suggests that our freedom and safety sometimes depend on people like Scott willing to do our dirty work our Christian faith sternly cautions us against such dangerous ends-justifies-the-means reasoning.

Due to much rough and sexually crude language and recurring graphic violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
